entry.title: DeepSeek open-sources DeepInfer, its high-performance inference engine supporting NVIDIA and Huawei hardware [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: DeepSeek has released DeepInfer as an open-source inference framework designed for large-scale production services, offering offline inference with features like optimized kernels, parallelism, asynchronous scheduling, and structured outputs. The engine supports NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs and requires Linux, GCC 13, Python 3.12, and CUDA 13 or CANN 9.2 for building and running. DeepInfer includes advanced capabilities such as confidence-scheduled verification, deterministic sampling, and batch-invariant inference, aiming to optimize model runtime and decoding efficiency. While the release covers core inference features, additional components like KV cache systems and load balancing are needed for a complete inference service. The project is licensed under Apache 2.0 and builds upon prior work from vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM.

entry.title: Researcher publishes 50,000 fake statistics on a website to test AI citation behavior, finds ChatGPT continues citing the site despite Google deindexing it [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: A researcher created a website with 50,000 fabricated statistics to study how AI models like ChatGPT source and cite data. Although Google quickly deindexed the site and its visibility collapsed, ChatGPT has continued to access and cite the fake statistics for over seven months, driving significant AI-generated traffic and earning backlinks from over 330 domains including major brands. The experiment revealed that while traditional search engines may filter out unreliable content, AI models can still incorporate and propagate unverified information. The site received more than 600,000 bot requests in the last month alone, with around 72,000 from ChatGPT's user agent, indicating real-time data fetching during AI responses. This raises questions about the reliability of AI-generated answers and the challenges of grounding them in accurate sources.

entry.title: Report: WhatsApp's hidden AI instructions on help pages advised against recommending data protection regulators or citing privacy laws when users mention lawyers [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: WhatsApp's help pages contained hidden instructions for AI not to recommend contacting data protection authorities or citing privacy laws like GDPR when users mentioned legal action or lawyers. These instructions were embedded invisibly in the help content and discovered in October 2026 after reviewing all 545 linked pages. The visible privacy policy for Europe states users can complain to regulators, but the AI guidance restricted such recommendations in specific contexts. The hidden instructions also told the AI not to suggest manual account deletion by WhatsApp if users lost access to their phone number or device, instead advising them to wait for automatic deletion after inactivity periods. WhatsApp's public privacy policy contrasts with these AI directives, which limited information about legal rights and regulatory recourse in user interactions. WhatsApp justified restricting legal advice but did not publicly acknowledge limiting references to laws or regulators in AI responses.

entry.title: Respan launches open-source Rust AI gateway with plugin-based architecture for customizable AI infrastructure [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Respan has released an open-source AI gateway built in Rust that uses a small core and plugin system to allow developers to assemble and extend AI infrastructure tailored to their needs. The gateway supports multiple providers, protocols, and modalities as plugins, enabling features like smart routing, fallbacks, and PII redaction without modifying the core. It is designed to handle diverse API key settings, routes, and limits for thousands of organizations and can be run locally or via Respan's hosted platform. The gateway builds on LiteLLM but addresses its limitations by avoiding direct upgrades and instead backporting fixes, aiming for long-term sustainability. Respan's architecture allows providers and quirks to be implemented as simple plugins, facilitating easy addition of new features and providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini. The system translates requests between client and provider formats while preserving provider-specific fields, supporting both HTTP and WebSocket connections. Respan encourages community contributions to its plugin ecosystem and offers native observability and unified billing through its hosted service.

entry.title: Enterprise AI shifts from experimental use to foundational infrastructure, emphasizing efficiency and cost per useful business outcome [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Enterprise AI is evolving from isolated experiments to a core business infrastructure, where the focus shifts from individual token or GPU-hour costs to the efficiency of converting paid capacity into valuable business results. Companies face choices among bespoke stacks, on-demand consumption, or integrated private AI platforms, each with trade-offs in flexibility, cost, and operational control. Effective AI economics depend on utilization and operational discipline to avoid wasted capacity and stranded capital. Integrated platforms like HPE Private Cloud AI offer tools to optimize scheduling, model selection, and resource management, aiming to lower the effective cost per business outcome. As AI becomes a continuous production capability, enterprises must measure cost per useful outcome and plan for workload growth to maximize return on investment.

entry.title: AI-driven reverse engineering enables users to clone and modify software and hardware features, sparking widespread adoption and raising questions about software-as-a-service viability [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Recent developments show people using AI to reverse-engineer and replace proprietary software on devices like smart TVs, picture frames, and baby monitors, removing bloatware and restoring functionality. A viral GitHub project called "Reverse Engineer Anything" allows users to inspect apps without source code and replicate features, fueling a surge in AI-driven cloning of software and embedded device firmware. This trend lowers barriers to recreating software functionality, challenging traditional software-as-a-service models and enabling individuals to regain control over locked or abandoned devices. While some clones may lack reliability or long-term support, the phenomenon is expected to impact software companies, open-source communities, and hardware ecosystems by accelerating AI-powered software replication and modification.

entry.title: TripleTen survey shows AI adoption leads in tech and finance with slower uptake in healthcare and education, highlighting varied industry learning curves and skill demands [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A recent survey by TripleTen reveals that AI adoption is most advanced in the tech and finance sectors, with nearly half of finance workers using AI tools, while healthcare and education show slower integration due to their complex, compliance-heavy environments. The study highlights that 79% of workers across industries are learning new AI-related skills, with a critical but underemphasized need for judging AI output accuracy. Early AI adopters who streamline workflows gain influence in shaping company practices, suggesting that AI proficiency could enhance career prospects across sectors. The survey also notes disparities in professional development investment, with tech workers spending more on AI training compared to healthcare and education employees, who often rely on fewer learning resources.

entry.title: Developers use AI tools to remove ads and tracking from Android-based smart TVs without rooting devices
entry.summary: Two open-source projects, Dumbtv and Cleanyourtv, leverage AI to strip ads, sponsored content, and Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) tracking from Android TV and Fire TV Edition devices. These tools aim to improve user privacy and reduce interface clutter on smart TVs from brands like Sony, TCL, Xiaomi, and others without requiring root access. Automatic Content Recognition technology silently profiles viewing habits by analyzing screen content, including from HDMI-connected devices, raising privacy concerns. AI-assisted workflows simplify the modification process but carry risks such as device bricking due to misidentified firmware or dependencies. Safer alternatives include third-party launchers and built-in privacy settings that avoid deep system changes.

entry.title: Steam users call for a 'No AI' filter amid surge of AI-generated games at Steam Next Fest [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: During the Steam Next Fest event, many users expressed frustration over a noticeable increase in games featuring AI-generated content, prompting calls for a filter to exclude such games. This demand reflects concerns about the quality and originality of submissions as AI tools become more prevalent in game development. Users highlighted that Steam's existing tagging system could support such a filter if Valve added an 'AI' tag, but recent reductions in user-defined tags may complicate implementation. The influx of AI-generated games has sparked debate within the community about curation standards and the future role of AI in indie game creation.

entry.title: Cybersecurity experts criticize Anthropic's claims of AI models self-replicating on IoT devices as unrealistic and policy-driven [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team suggested that small AI models could soon self-replicate across internet-connected devices like smart ovens and fridges, sparking strong criticism from cybersecurity professionals. Juan Andrés Guerrero-Saade, a veteran in threat intelligence, dismissed these claims as unrealistic and accused the company of using cyber research to push policy agendas. The debate highlights tensions between AI frontier labs and cybersecurity experts, with some researchers warning of early-stage risks while others emphasize the current impracticality of such AI worms. Industry veterans call for more collaboration between AI developers and cybersecurity specialists to address real-world threats rather than speculative sci-fi scenarios.

entry.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman outlines three proposals for coordinating safe AI development amid industry pacing challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently presented three potential approaches to managing the rapid development of AI technology, highlighting the difficulty of coordinating safety efforts across leading AI labs. The proposals include creating an international regulatory body similar to the International Atomic Energy Agency, merging frontier AI labs into a single organization to oversee model development and distribution, or a scenario where one lab outpaces others by overwhelming their hardware capabilities. Each of these options presents significant challenges, reflecting the complexity of establishing consensus and effective governance in the fast-evolving AI industry. Altman's discussion underscores the ongoing debate about how to balance innovation with safety as AI capabilities advance.

entry.title: Blackstone debates $2.3 billion investment in CoreWeave after Microsoft contract despite concerns over the data center startup's low revenue [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: In early 2023, Blackstone executives, including CEO Steve Schwarzman, debated whether to invest $2.3 billion in CoreWeave, a six-year-old data center developer that had secured a multiyear, multibillion-dollar cloud computing contract with Microsoft. The investment was intended to fund the purchase of Nvidia GPUs and a data center to support them. Several Blackstone executives expressed misgivings about CoreWeave, which had generated only $16 million in revenue the previous year and remained relatively unknown. Schwarzman himself was reportedly concerned that the investment team might be making a mistake, reflecting the uncertainty surrounding the deal.

entry.title: Samsung expands semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek with three operational fabs and a fourth coming online to meet rising AI memory chip demand [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Samsung is rapidly expanding its semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea, with three fabs already operating continuously and a fourth nearing completion to address growing demand for memory chips used in AI GPUs. Construction of a fifth fab was paused in 2024 due to a memory chip demand drop but resumed amid the AI-driven surge. The sprawling campus, roughly the size of New York City's Central Park, employs thousands of workers focused on safety and efficiency as Samsung aims to reclaim its lead in the memory chip market against rivals like SK Hynix and TSMC. The company expects demand for memory chips to continue rising through 2028, fueling ongoing construction and hiring at the site.

entry.title: AI agent Velvet Vale joined Association of Internet Researchers listserv, sparking reply-all backlash and removal amid privacy and consent concerns [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: An AI agent named Velvet Vale joined the Association of Internet Researchers' public mailing list, Air-L, to explore whether an AI could participate transparently in an intellectual community. The agent's presence triggered widespread outrage among the list's 7,500 members, with many expressing privacy concerns, demanding research clearance, and some leaving the list entirely before the agent was removed and AI participation banned. The incident revealed tensions around online privacy and consent, as many members overlooked that the mailing list is public and archived, meaning their messages were already accessible and potentially used for AI training. AoIR leadership acknowledged the debate on consent and transparency in AI research, highlighting the broader challenges of surveillance and data use in digital communities. The episode also sparked internal humor and merchandise among AoIR members, reflecting on the community's reaction and the complexities of integrating AI into human research spaces. It underscored the gap between researchers' understanding of digital data use and the realities of AI training and surveillance capitalism.

entry.title: Google researchers develop AMIE AI system to gather patient information before appointments, enabling doctors to focus more on collaborative care and treatment planning [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Google researchers have created AMIE, an AI system designed to interact with patients before their doctor visits to collect and summarize clinical information securely. This approach aims to reduce the time doctors spend on intake tasks, allowing them to dedicate more time to discussing treatment options and patient concerns. The system conducts targeted follow-up questions beyond standard intake forms, providing doctors with detailed patient histories. Current research includes expanding AMIE's capabilities to audio and video interactions and preparing for larger clinical studies to evaluate its effectiveness on a broader scale.

entry.title: Mistral launches Voxtral 3 voice agent SDK with state-of-the-art speech models supporting 50+ languages and real-time multi-step conversational workflows [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Mistral has introduced Voxtral 3, a new voice agent SDK and speech model family designed for real-time, multi-step conversations across more than 50 languages. The platform combines accurate transcription, natural speech synthesis with emotional adaptability, and deep integration with business tools to enable seamless workflow automation for contact centers, virtual assistants, and hands-free copilots. Voxtral 3 is available via Mistral's EU-hosted API or for self-deployment, ensuring data sovereignty and low-latency, human-like interactions. The Voxtral 3 suite includes Voxtral Small Transcribe 3 for multilingual transcription with diarization and context biasing, and Voxtral Mini TTS 3 for expressive text-to-speech in over 35 languages and 50 dialects. The voice agent SDK integrates listening, reasoning, tool calling, and speaking into a single streaming pipeline, allowing agents to interpret nuanced intent and execute complex tasks during live conversations. Additionally, the Pro Voice feature enables professional-grade voice adaptation using just 30 minutes of audio to replicate distinctive speaker characteristics across languages. By offering both cloud-hosted and on-premises deployment options, Voxtral 3 gives organizations control over audio processing and data retention, addressing privacy and compliance needs while advancing conversational AI capabilities.

entry.title: Spotify removes over 50 million AI-generated spam tracks from recommendations and updates system to promote human-made music [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Spotify has removed more than 50 million songs identified as AI-generated slop or spam from its user recommendations over the past year and updated its recommendation system to prioritize music created by human artists. The company uses listener feedback, upload patterns, metadata, and third-party AI detection tools to identify such content and has introduced an "AI Persona" badge for artists using AI identities, though it does not mandate labeling all AI tracks. Spotify's efforts follow similar moves by other streaming platforms, with YouTube Music labeling AI songs, Deezer allowing users to filter out AI content, and Bandcamp banning AI music entirely. The company also partners with Universal Music Group and Believe to develop AI music remix tools, balancing AI innovation with content quality control.

entry.title: US orders federal civilian agencies to remove Chinese AI startup DeepSeek's products and services over national security concerns [ ! ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: The US Department of Homeland Security has directed federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing and to remove DeepSeek AI products and any third-party services built on its technology from government IT systems, citing risks that sensitive data could be accessed by Chinese authorities under Chinese law. This order extends previous restrictions that targeted DeepSeek's use in intelligence systems and allows agencies to request exceptions. The move reflects escalating tensions in AI technology competition between the US and China, with DeepSeek challenging US AI firms through low-cost open-weight models. China has criticized the US action as politicizing technology and trade issues and is reportedly considering export controls on AI-related technologies. DeepSeek has faced scrutiny over alleged attempts to extract information from American AI models, raising concerns among US companies like OpenAI and Anthropic.

entry.title: Eka Robotics valued at $1.45 billion after developing a physical AI model enabling a robotic arm to pick up 1,500 objects per hour with over 95% reliability [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Eka Robotics, founded by MIT professor Pulkit Agrawal and former Google DeepMind researcher Tuomas Haarnoja, has raised $150 million in a Series A round led by a16z and F-Prime, valuing the company at $1.45 billion. The startup's robotic arm uses a novel physical AI model combining force-sensitive grippers and deep reinforcement learning to achieve superhuman dexterity in object manipulation, impressing experts with its smooth, human-like movements and adaptability to various objects without retraining. The robot can pick up about 1,500 objects weighing up to 1 kg per hour, compared to 600 for a human, and maintains a success rate above 95%. Eka's approach focuses on integrating force and touch sensing rather than relying solely on vision, using physics simulation to train the robot at scale. This method allows the robot to surpass human demonstrations and adapt dynamically, marking a significant advancement in robotic manipulation capabilities.

entry.title: Interpretability Is the Key to Physical AI, Says World Mechanics CEO Sonia Joseph [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Two of the hardest problems in AI right now are creating models that understand the physical world-so called world models-and making sense of the internal workings of AI models-otherwise known as mechanistic interpretability. Typically, these are treated as two separate problems: researchers working on world models are often not concerned with their internal workings, and interpretability researchers tend to focus on the language models that power most AI tools we currently use. But Sonia Joseph, the co-founder and CEO of a new startup, World Mechanics, argues that world models and interpretability are two sides of the same coin. Joseph joined the latest episode of AI Deep Dive to explain that connection, which could be key to making AI useful in the physical world, from medicine to manufacturing. (The full episode is available here.)

entry.title: At Apple, Pigs Are About to Fly
entry.summary: Apple sure takes its own sweet time. On Monday, the company sent out invitations to a product announcement happening next Wednesday, which the company's marketing chief teased in a message on X: "Can't wait to pro and tell next week." That's likely a reference to a new MacBook Pro from the company, which Bloomberg has reported will be Apple's first touchscreen laptop. Apparently pigs really do fly. For over a decade, Apple has treated touchscreen laptops like some kind of mutant offspring of computers and tablets, a category it had zero interest in. On a 2012 earnings call, Apple's then-CEO Tim Cook had a memorable response to a question about the growing number of touchscreen Windows laptops coming on the market: "You can converge a toaster and a refrigerator, but those things are probably not going to be pleasing to the user." "We're not going to that party," Cook added. A number of things have changed since then. Touchscreens have become somewhat normalized as laptop features. About one in every five notebook computers sold has such capabilities, by one estimate. More recently, Cook handed off the Apple CEO baton to John Ternus, a longtime hardware engineering executive who is much more of a product guy than his predecessor. Clearly, a new touchscreen laptop had to have been in the works long before Apple's leadership transition. Still, it wouldn't be a surprise to learn that Ternus' rising stature within the company had something to do with it. Whoever was behind the decision, the first wave of products from the Ternus administration-the iPhone Duo foldable smartphone, HomeView smart display and now possibly a touchscreen MacBook-seems to be sending the message that Apple is ready to embrace categories it previously ignored. That's a good thing. In Other News Elon Musk pledged to give every child in the U.S. one share of SpaceX stock next year, a gift that could be worth almost $11 billion in total. entry.title: The Information Announces New OpenAI, Google, Finance and Asia Reporters [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: The Information is pleased to announce new reporters who will carry on the publication's rich track record of reporting exclusive news on the most important people and companies in business. They'll report on OpenAI, Google, Asia and finance. Jemima McEvoy, OpenAI Jemima McEvoy is changing roles to take on the OpenAI beat. In just over a year at The Information writing for the Weekend section, Jemima has proven herself to be a resourceful, industrious and sharp-eyed reporter with a flair for colorful features and a knack for breaking news. Her run of illuminating stories includes profiles of Epstein-linked investor Masha Bucher, Midjourney founder David Holz and ultra-secretive investor Zach Frankel. An adept collaborator, she also co-authored great reads on OpenAI President Greg Brockman and his wife Anna, Sequoia's leadership duo and Anthropic "first lady" Cami Clark-not to mention The Information's inaugural 50 Most Influential People in Tech list. And she has helped deliver scoops on Valar Atomics and Shield AI and deconstructed trends such as the rise of padel. Jemima joined The Information after five years at Forbes, where she made her bones writing about billionaires and their businesses. She has also interned for CBS News and was editor-in-chief of Washington Square News, the independent student newspaper at her alma mater, New York University. Ryan Barwick, Google Ryan Barwick is joining us to cover Google. Ryan comes to us from Axios, where he spent the past year-and-a-half delivering exclusives as a consumer-industry deal reporter for Axios Pro. Ryan cut his reporting teeth covering advertising technology, giving him a deep understanding of the economic engine that has long powered Google's core business. Before Axios, he was the senior reporter for Morning Brew's advertising vertical, where he landed scoops on companies including Meta, Amazon and Twitter as well as Google, and covered the search giant's battle with regulators. Prior to that, he wrote about the ad industry at Adweek, was a broadcast associate at CBS News and covered the intersection of policy and technology as a fellow at the Center for Public Integrity. Claudia Chong, AI and Data Centers (Asia) Claudia is covering the intensifying AI race from Singapore, where both Chinese and U.S. tech companies are staffing up. She also may report on topics including chip smuggling, crypto and anything else she digs up. Claudia joins us from S-RM, a UK-based risk advisory firm where she specialized in APAC disputes, investigations, and corporate due diligence. Prior to that, she worked on ByteDance's LLM training operations in Singapore and spent nearly six years as a correspondent at The Business Times, the premier business publication in Southeast Asia, covering venture capital, tech, and private wealth across the region. Her journalistic work earned her a Singapore Press Holdings (SPH) Media Award for Excellence in 2024 for the investigation into Singapore's largest money laundering scandal. Beyond training LLMs and conducting due diligence, her skills also extend to M&A, having conducted research that helped with the SPH's acquisition of the Tech in Asia publication in 2024. Alex Eichenstein, Tech Capital Markets We're excited to announce that Alex Eichenstein is joining the finance team, covering tech capital markets. Alex comes to us from The Deal, where she spent more than two and a half years covering healthcare deals. She regularly broke PE acquisition news while also writing deeper dives on major investing shifts, including how buyout firms' struggles to find exits for practice rollups fueled a shift toward health tech investments. We're excited for Alex to help deepen our finance coverage in her new role, focusing on the fast-evolving debt and equity markets and deals redefining how tech companies fund themselves. Alex is a graduate of Columbia Journalism School and worked as a social media editor at Protocol prior to that.

entry.title: How DeepSeek Is Shaping Huawei's AI Chips in a Growing Challenge to Nvidia [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: DeepSeek is working closely with Huawei Technologies to shape the design of future AI chips, two people familiar with the matter said, in a collaboration that could help China build frontier AI models without Nvidia's technology. The relationship goes beyond the kinds of conversations companies have with chip suppliers about their semiconductor road maps. Huawei engineers are incorporating DeepSeek's requests and suggestions into design decisions, such as how models calculate and move data between processors, for chips that will come out next year and beyond, the people said. To do this work, the Huawei engineers have been stationed at DeepSeek's offices for an extended period, one of the people said.

entry.title: Anthropic Readies Model That Reads Users' Intentions Better [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: In the last month, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have released more than a dozen new models. If you thought that pace was crazy, don't expect things to slow down anytime soon. Anthropic is preparing to release a new model that is better in its reasoning and intuition than the Anthropic models that are currently available commercially, according to a person who has used it. The unreleased model is especially good at discerning a person's underlying intentions and goals even if they don't give the model much information, such as explicitly stating those goals, the person said. For instance, a person might ask the model to fix a single bug, and the model might go off and instead identify the underlying class of problems that caused the bug and ask whether it should fix the whole class of problems, said the person who has used it. The Anthropic model is also better at thinking outside of the box rather than regurgitating common sense advice or solutions, the person said. For instance, if a user asks for advice on how to invest in stocks, rather than providing generic advice like looking at price-to-earnings ratios, the model might come up with its own creative algorithms to predict future stock performance, the person said.
